He also developed calculus, in a long dispute with Gottfried Leibniz about priority, built the first practical reflecting telescope in 1668 and showed with prisms that white light is made of colours, published in Opticks in 1704.

Newton became President of the Royal Society and Master of the Royal Mint, and was knighted in 1705. He wrote that if he had seen further, it was by standing on the shoulders of giants. He was buried in Westminster Abbey.

articles.title: Albert Einstein
articles.description: The physicist who reshaped our view of space and time.
articles.content:
Albert Einstein (1879–1955) was a German-born physicist, born in Ulm. In 1905, while working in the patent office in Bern, Switzerland, he published four groundbreaking papers, including on the photoelectric effect, Brownian motion and special relativity, which included the equation E = mc². That year is called his miracle year.

In 1915 he completed general relativity, a new theory of gravity that was confirmed in 1919 when the bending of starlight was seen during a solar eclipse and made him world famous. He received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1921 for explaining the photoelectric effect, a key step in quantum theory, though he remained sceptical of some of its implications.

Einstein left Germany when the Nazis came to power in 1933 and settled in Princeton, New Jersey. In 1939 he signed a letter to President Roosevelt warning about the possibility of atomic weapons, and later campaigned for peace. He also loved playing the violin.

articles.title: Marie Curie
articles.description: The pioneer of radioactivity and the first woman Nobel laureate.
articles.content:
Marie Curie (1867–1934) was born Maria Skłodowska in Warsaw, and moved to Paris in 1891 to study at the Sorbonne, since women could not attend university in Russian-ruled Poland. She married the physicist Pierre Curie, and together they investigated the mysterious rays discovered by Henri Becquerel, which she named radioactivity.

In 1898 they discovered two new elements, polonium, named after her homeland, and radium. In 1903 she became the first woman to win a Nobel Prize, in Physics, shared with Pierre and Becquerel, and in 1911 she won a second, in Chemistry, making her the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.

During World War I she developed mobile X-ray units, called little Curies, to help wounded soldiers. She founded the Radium Institute in Paris. She died in 1934 from an illness related to her long exposure to radiation, and her notebooks are still radioactive today. Her daughter Irène also won a Nobel Prize.

articles.title: Galileo Galilei
articles.description: The astronomer who turned the telescope to the sky.
articles.content:
Galileo Galilei (1564–1642) was an Italian scientist from Pisa, often called the father of modern science. He studied motion, discovering that a pendulum swings with a regular rhythm, and showed that falling objects accelerate at the same rate regardless of their weight. The story that he dropped balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa is probably a legend.

In 1609 he made improvements to the newly invented telescope and turned it to the sky. He saw mountains and craters on the Moon, the four largest moons of Jupiter, now called the Galilean moons, the phases of Venus and sunspots, and many more stars in the Milky Way. These discoveries supported Copernicus's idea that the Earth orbits the Sun.

His support for this view brought him into conflict with the Catholic Church. In 1633 he was tried by the Inquisition and forced to renounce it, and he spent the rest of his life under house arrest. The Vatican formally acknowledged errors in his case in 1992.

articles.title: Nikola Tesla
articles.description: The inventor who electrified the world with alternating current.
articles.content:
Nikola Tesla (1856–1943) was an inventor and engineer, born in Smiljan, then part of the Austrian Empire and now in Croatia, to a Serbian family. He moved to the United States in 1884 and briefly worked for Thomas Edison.

Tesla designed the alternating current, or AC, induction motor and the systems for generating and distributing AC power. His partnership with George Westinghouse and the success of AC over Edison's direct current in the so-called War of the Currents led to the first big hydroelectric plant at Niagara Falls in 1895. He also invented the Tesla coil in 1891, worked on radio and remote control, and held about 300 patents.

Tesla dreamed of wireless transmission of electricity, and his Wardenclyffe Tower project on Long Island was never finished. He died poor in a New York hotel. The unit of magnetic flux density, the tesla, is named after him, as is the electric car company.

articles.title: Michael Faraday
articles.description: The self-taught genius of electricity and magnetism.
articles.content:
Michael Faraday (1791–1867) was an English scientist who came from a poor family and had little formal schooling. As a boy he was apprenticed to a bookbinder, where he read the books he bound, and after attending lectures by the chemist Humphry Davy, he became Davy's assistant at the Royal Institution in London.

In 1821 he built the first electric motor, and in 1831 he discovered electromagnetic induction, the principle that a changing magnetic field produces an electric current, which is the basis of electric generators and transformers. He also discovered the laws of electrolysis, invented the Faraday cage, which shields against electric fields, and introduced the idea of fields of force.

Faraday was a great communicator: in 1825 he began the Royal Institution Christmas Lectures for young people, which continue today, and his series The Chemical History of a Candle is a classic. He declined a knighthood and the presidency of the Royal Society. The unit of capacitance, the farad, is named after him.

articles.title: Stephen Hawking
articles.description: The physicist who explored black holes and the universe.
articles.content:
Stephen Hawking (1942–2018) was a British theoretical physicist, born in Oxford, on the 300th anniversary of Galileo's death. At the age of 21 he was diagnosed with motor neurone disease, and doctors expected him to live only a few years, but he lived for another 55, becoming one of the most famous scientists in the world.

He worked on black holes and the origin of the universe. With Roger Penrose he showed that general relativity implies singularities, and in 1974 he showed that black holes are not completely black but emit a faint radiation, now called Hawking radiation. He was Lucasian Professor of Mathematics at Cambridge from 1979 to 2009, the post once held by Isaac Newton.

His book A Brief History of Time (1988) sold more than 10 million copies. As he lost the ability to speak, he used a computer-based speech device. He died on 14 March 2018, which is Pi Day and Albert Einstein's birthday.

articles.title: Al-Khwarizmi
articles.description: The Baghdad scholar who gave us algebra and the algorithm.
articles.content:
Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi (about 780–850) was a Persian scholar from Khwarazm, in Central Asia, who worked at the House of Wisdom in Baghdad under the Abbasid caliph al-Ma'mun. He was a mathematician, astronomer and geographer.

Around 820 he wrote The Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing, which gave step-by-step methods for solving linear and quadratic equations. Its Arabic title includes the word al-jabr, from which the word algebra comes. Another of his books introduced the Hindu numerals, including zero, to the Arabic-speaking world, and the Latin translation spread them to Europe as the numerals we use today.

The Latinised form of his name, Algoritmi, gave us the word algorithm. He also prepared astronomical tables and improved the world map of Ptolemy. His work was a foundation of mathematics in both the Islamic world and Europe.

articles.title: Ibn al-Haytham
articles.description: The father of modern optics.
articles.content:
Ibn al-Haytham, known in Europe as Alhazen (about 965–1040), was an Arab scholar born in Basra, in present-day Iraq, who worked mainly in Cairo. He was a mathematician, astronomer and physicist, and is often called the father of modern optics.

In his seven-volume Book of Optics, written between about 1011 and 1021, he showed by experiments that we see because light reflects from objects into the eye, not because the eye sends out rays, as the ancient Greek scholars Euclid and Ptolemy had argued. He studied reflection and refraction, described the camera obscura, and explained how the eye works.

He also stressed the importance of testing ideas with careful experiments, an approach that is a forerunner of the scientific method. The Latin translation of his book influenced European scientists such as Roger Bacon and Johannes Kepler.

articles.title: Rosalind Franklin
articles.description: The scientist whose X-ray image revealed the shape of DNA.
articles.content:
Rosalind Franklin (1920–1958) was an English chemist and X-ray crystallographer. After studying at Cambridge and working in Paris, in 1951 she joined King's College London, where she used X-ray diffraction to study the structure of DNA.

In May 1952, with her student Raymond Gosling, she took the famous Photograph 51, a very clear X-ray image of DNA that showed a helical structure. Her data and measurements, which were shown to James Watson and Francis Crick without her knowledge, helped them build their double-helix model in 1953. Watson, Crick and Maurice Wilkins received the Nobel Prize in 1962; she had died four years earlier at the age of 37, and Nobel Prizes are not awarded after death.

Franklin also did important work on the structure of coal and graphite, and on viruses such as the tobacco mosaic virus. Her contribution is now widely recognised.

articles.title: The Nobel Prize
articles.description: The world's most famous award for achievement.
articles.content:
The Nobel Prizes were established by the will of the Swedish chemist and inventor Alfred Nobel, who invented dynamite in 1867 and died in 1896. He left most of his fortune to fund prizes for those who had conferred the greatest benefit on humankind. They were first awarded in 1901.

The original five prizes were in Physics, Chemistry, Physiology or Medicine, Literature and Peace. In 1968 the Swedish central bank added a prize in Economic Sciences. The prizes are awarded each year on 10 December, the anniversary of Nobel's death, in Stockholm, with the Peace Prize in Oslo. Each carries a gold medal, a diploma and prize money of about 11 million Swedish kronor.

Over a thousand people and organisations have received them. Marie Curie won twice, and the youngest laureate, Malala Yousafzai, was 17 when she received the Peace Prize in 2014. The physicist Lev Landau, born in Baku, won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1962.

articles.title: The International System of Units
articles.description: The metric measures that scientists share worldwide.
articles.content:
The International System of Units, or SI, is the modern form of the metric system and the standard used by scientists and most countries around the world. It has seven base units: the metre for length, the kilogram for mass, the second for time, the ampere for electric current, the kelvin for temperature, the mole for amount of substance and the candela for luminous intensity.

The metric system was created during the French Revolution in the 1790s, when the metre was defined as one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator. In 2019 the definitions were changed so that all seven units are based on fixed values of natural constants, for instance the second on the vibrations of a caesium atom, and the kilogram on the Planck constant, instead of a physical metal cylinder kept in France.

Prefixes such as kilo, milli and micro make it easy to switch between sizes. The United States, Liberia and Myanmar are the only countries that have not officially adopted the metric system for everyday use.

articles.title: Fossil Fuels
articles.description: Coal, oil and gas: energy from ancient life.
articles.content:
Fossil fuels are coal, oil and natural gas, formed over millions of years from the remains of ancient plants and marine organisms buried under layers of sediment and subjected to heat and pressure. Much of the world's coal comes from swamp forests of the Carboniferous period, about 300 to 360 million years ago.

They contain energy that came from the Sun, captured by ancient plants. Coal powered the Industrial Revolution, oil became the fuel of transport after the invention of the internal combustion engine, and natural gas heats homes and generates electricity. Together they still provide about 80% of the world's energy.

Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide and is the main cause of climate change. They are also non-renewable on human timescales. Countries are now working to shift toward renewable sources such as solar and wind, though the transition will take decades. Azerbaijan, whose oil fields near Baku were among the first developed, has long relied on oil and gas.

articles.title: Time
articles.description: What clocks measure and physics wonders about.
articles.content:
Time is the ongoing sequence of events from past to present to future, and one of the basic quantities in physics. It is measured by clocks, which count regular repeating events, such as the swing of a pendulum or the vibrations of atoms.

Ancient people used the Sun and stars: sundials and water clocks were used in Egypt, Babylon and China. Mechanical clocks appeared in Europe in the 13th and 14th centuries, and in 1656 Christiaan Huygens built the first pendulum clock. Today the second is defined by 9,192,631,770 vibrations of a caesium-133 atom, and the best atomic clocks lose less than a second over hundreds of millions of years.

According to Einstein's relativity, time is not absolute: it passes more slowly for objects moving fast or near strong gravity, an effect called time dilation, which GPS satellites must correct for. Why time seems to flow in one direction only, the arrow of time, is still debated in physics.

articles.title: Aristotle
articles.description: The Greek philosopher who studied nearly everything.
articles.content:
Aristotle (384–322 BCE) was a Greek philosopher and scientist, born in Stagira in northern Greece. He studied in Plato's Academy in Athens for about twenty years and later became the tutor of the young Alexander the Great. In 335 BCE he founded his own school, the Lyceum.

He wrote about logic, physics, biology, ethics, politics, poetry and more. In logic, he developed the syllogism, a form of reasoning. In biology, he observed and classified animals, dissecting and describing about 500 species, and studied marine life on the island of Lesbos, so he is sometimes called the first biologist.

Some of his scientific ideas were wrong, for instance that heavier objects fall faster and that the Earth is the centre of the universe, but they dominated thinking for nearly two thousand years, until the Scientific Revolution. His works were preserved and studied by scholars in the Islamic world and later in medieval Europe.

articles.title: Nanotechnology
articles.description: Engineering at the scale of atoms and molecules.
articles.content:
Nanotechnology is the science and engineering of materials and devices at the nanoscale, about one to 100 nanometres. A nanometre is one billionth of a metre: a human hair is about 80,000 nanometres wide, and a DNA molecule about two nanometres.

The physicist Richard Feynman inspired the field with his 1959 talk There's Plenty of Room at the Bottom, and the Japanese scientist Norio Taniguchi used the term in 1974. The invention of the scanning tunnelling microscope in 1981 allowed scientists to see and move individual atoms, and in 1991 Sumio Iijima discovered carbon nanotubes, which are much stronger than steel for their weight.

At this scale materials can have new properties. Nanotechnology is used in computer chips, sunscreens, stain-resistant fabrics and new medicines that deliver drugs directly to cells. Researchers are also studying its safety, and its possible uses in energy, water purification and medicine.
